question: What is the meaning of analysis of the demolition acquisition in relation to material layers, materials?
description: The analysis of the demolition acquisition (DA) in relation to material layers refers to the process of assessing and documenting the types and masses of materials present in a building before demolition. This assessment helps in understanding the composition of the building's materials, which is crucial for planning the demolition and subsequent waste disposal. The DA involves collecting data on the building's materials, often through visual inspection and chemical analysis, to determine the types and quantities of materials embedded in the building. This information is then used to calculate the mass of certain types of waste based on the volume of the respective building components and default material densities. The analysis of material layers specifically refers to examining the different layers of materials within the building, such as walls, foundations, and other structural elements, to identify and document the materials present in each layer. This detailed understanding of material layers is essential for effective waste management and recycling during the demolition process.

to be stated that the aim of this paper is to test the transferability of the 
MP method, initially developed for new construction, on an existing 
building with regards to the material acquisition methods. Accordingly, 
the focus lies on the limitations and potentials of the material acquisition 
methods and not on the correctness of the acquired data. However, since 
the UMA is a very thorough assessment using destructive methods, the 
results are expected to be very accurate and correct. However, an 
assessment of the data uncertainties, which would help defining the 
reliability of the MP results, and a comparison with the actually disposed 
materials would be supportive, but were not conducted. 
5. Discussion 
This research has shown, that through the application of the MP- 
method, valuable results regarding the sustainability of buildings are 
generated. However, it has to be stated that the applied MP-method is a 
basic method, which should be refined and enriched with more influ­
encing parameters such as e.g. the deconstruction potential and location 
of a material within the building. The deconstruction potential could 
show how good two building components (e.g. a wall and a slab) can be 
separated from each other, without demolishing the components, thus 
enabling a higher reuse potential of the components. The location plays 
a crucial role, since it is more effortful to deconstruct a high-rise building 
than a single-storey building. A differentiation between the reuse and 
recycling potential should be conducted within the MP-method, since 
reuse of materials or elements requires less processing than recycling 
and therefore should be preferred at the deconstruction of the building. 
Moreover, the monetary value of the materials in existing buildings 
should be integrated into the MP assessments in order to enable a 
comparison of the prices of new and reused or recycled materials. Apart 
from that, using indicators from IBO might not always be correct, since 
this information is for new constructions and not for existing buildings. 
For the MP usually all the materials are included in the assessment, 
however it needs to be questioned, if this accuracy-level is necessary, 
since a detailed acquisition is an effortful and time-consuming process, 
as demonstrated within this work. Future research should address 
determining of the needed accuracy-level of the acquisition in the scope 
of a pre-demolition audit. Therefore, a clear description of the content of 
the MP for the end-of-life-phase is required. However, as shown in the 
results, in order to obtain correct results, it is necessary to either be very 
careful while acquisition or to compare the results with another acqui­
sition, since mistakes can occur easily. Apart from the fact that the 
acquisition is a very effortful process, to be conducted at the end-of-life 
stage of the building, it needs to be questioned if the existence of the MP 
in the pre-demolition phase has any value and if it helps to optimize the 
end-of-life phase of a material or element. It is obvious, that in the pre- 
demolition phase the state-of-the-art waste streams cannot be changed 
easily, due to the restricted time, which is why the MP should already be 
existing before the demolition-decision of a building. The existence of an 
MP in earlier stages, might enable the planning of the final stage of an 
element or material, thus might enable higher reuse or recycling rates. 
However, invasive methods, as applied within the UMA, can only be 
utilized, if the building is a demolition object.

Within this 
paper, the MP-assessment method was applied on a real use case, where 
through destructive methods the separability of materials was analyzed 
on selected building elements as well as documented. As this research is 
based on real data acquired on site, as described in section 2.3, it delivers 
reliable information regarding the separability of materials. As the 
proposed MP-assessment method was initially developed for the build­
ing design stage, as described in 2.1, the quality of the materials did not 
play a crucial role. However, for existing buildings the quality has to be 
integrated in the assessment since at the end-of-life stage the quality of 
material might vary. Accordingly, within the adapted MP, the assigned 
grades from 1 to 5 are downgraded if a material has a lower quality at 
the end-of-life stage. 
2.3. Data acquisition methods 
The proposed BIM-based MP-method requires an extension in terms 
of data assessment and technology, in order to allow the assessment of 
the geometry and material composition as well as to obtain the required 
parameters for generating an MP. For the investigated use case, the 
existing planning documents (from 1993) were not up-to-date. Within 
the planning documents, only the assembly of the foundation was 
recorded. However, since the documents were old, a verification was 
necessary. Accordingly, the following data acquisition methods were 
applied: geometry acquisition with laser scanning and the resulting 
point cloud for the generation of the BIM-model, material identification 
from the demolition acquisition (DA) perspective and from the urban 
mining assessment (UMA) perspective. Both material acquisition 
methods were conducted through on-site inspections, wherefore also the 
existing documentation was used for preparation of investigations. Since 
the building was planned to be demolished in the near future, invasive 
methods could be applied to obtain the exact material composition. The 
on-site inspection of the DA was conducted in 5 h, whereas the UMA 
took 25 h. Manual tools such as a hammer and chisel were used. 
The DA – a survey of the building in the context of a pre-demolition 
waste audit, is a mandatory acquisition in Austria for demolition objects 
with a volume of more than 3500 m3. The pre-demolition audit for this 
building was conducted while the occupants were in the building and 
contains of assumptions without using too invasive methods. The pre- 
demolition waste audit is prescribed by the Austrian norm “¨ONORM 
EN ISO, 20140–32” (¨ONORM EN ISO, 20140–32, 2014) and has the aim 
of assessing the waste masses of each material embedded in the building 
as well as detecting hazardous materials e.g. asbestos, since they require 
a special demolition and disposal procedure. Within the DA, the type of 
material was assessed either visually at the on-site inspection or based 
on additional chemical analyses based on samples taken at the on-site 
inspection. The mass of certain types of waste was calculated based on 
the volume of the respective building components and respective default 
material densities for the respective materials. As the DA was conducted 
within the scope of the pre-demolition audit, the results were mapped to 
the type of waste which is linked to “key-numbers”, whereby each 
key-number represents a specific building waste type. 
The UMA included a particularly thorough analysis of the building 
by applying invasive methods such as cutting and drilling, which was 
possible due to the move of the occupants to their new facility. The aim 
of this assessment was to identify the material composition as accurate 
as possible by considering all elements of the building. Thereby the 
exterior walls were investigated in detail at one point of the building, 
where the metal cladding of the use case could be removed. From this 
punctual investigation it was assumed, that the composition of the 
exterior walls is the same. For the metal cladding, this assumption could 
be verified through the on-site inspection. The layer behind the cladding 
could only be verified through knocking. As the walls were assumed to 
compose of three layers, the third material could be verified from the 
interior. The same method was used for all building components, which 
were accessible (roof, foundation and interior walls). For the foundation 
some information could be obtained from the planning documents, 
though, the exact composition was obtained from drillings.
